And I started looking closer at the seam that extended all the way around the middle of the toy, as I lowered one of the arms to inspect the seam where the head and arm met, that area just started coming apart.  And it only took minimal pressure for it to continue to rip.  So then I looked at the same area where the head and shoulder/arm met on the other side, and the same thing happened. It just started coming apart.  You can see what I mean in the 4th and 5th photos.  This should not happen with any squishy toy, or any other toy for that matter.  I consider this a safety concern and am giving this toy one star for this reason.

The battery for the copter charged quickly. The batteries for the controls come with, but you'll need a tiny screwdriver to get them in.

Flying inside is easier than outside, though completely not recommended. The copter is so light, it is susceptible to the gentlest wind. The controls are very hair-sensitive, making it difficult to steer with any accuracy. As such, fly in a large field. Otherwise, expect it stuck in a tree, land on a roof, or be busted up on the street.

Extra blades are included. After a few crashes, I can see they'll be necessary. I don't expect it to be durable with any extended use.

I'm giving it three stars because it does work as advertised. Overall, however, I'm unimpressed.

text_fidelity_a:
Radio Flyer (My 1st 2-in-1 Wagon, Red Is this easy to assemble? Apparently! My 3 little guys put it together while I was cooking supper. So, it's also quick to assemble. They did a great job, minus putting the handle on backwards. Though I've tried to take the wheels off to move the handle around, I've been unsuccessful. That hasn't kept them from having a great time with it, though. My older 2 have pulled my 3 year old around in it, and he has had a great time loading and unloading his stuffed animals. The good news is, even if put on backwards, the handle still locks!

This wagon is on the small side. My 3 year old is small for his age, but he still has to squeeze in there. I wouldn't recommend older than that riding in it due to fearing it will break. It also flips over pretty easily, so I don't recommend too much riding in it, period, especially for the younger little ones. It IS great for pulling things like stuffed animals and books around, though.

This wagon is plastic, like most of the other Radio Flyer toys these days. We have a few of them, and they have always been well loved and played with by my boys. Despite being plastic, they have proved to be very sturdy so far.

Overall, you really can't go wrong if this wagon is for pulling little toys around. It will provide hours of (semi)quiet fun for your little one. If you're wanting something to pull a child around in, though, I'd go a different route.
text_fidelity_b: Radio Flyer (My 1st 2-in-1 Wagon, Red

Klutz Painted Rocks Craft Kit Multicolor, 10.5" Length x 0.75" Width x 8.5" Height This craft kit comes with a book on rock painting, eight acrylic paints, one paint brush, four pairs of self-adhesive googly eyes, and one rock. The kit is for ages 6 and up. The 40 page book comes with instructions on how to use the acrylic paints and included 28 step-by-step instructions for creating various paintings, from animals and flowers to various people, foods, and more. The book also contained pictures of other rock painting ideas but left it to the reader to figure out the steps needed to get the finished product. Most of these were pretty obvious and were similar to previous step-by-step projects.

The acrylic paints are white, black, blue, yellow, red, orange, green, and purple. Some of the designs required mixing these colors to make a new color, and adults may need to help younger kids with this. The paints had something in them to slow the drying time a little (so more like 30 minutes for dry to the touch rather than just a few minutes more typical for acrylic). This allowed for more time to make changes or mixing color on the rock.

The value in this kit is mainly the book as you only get one rock (thankfully...they're easy enough to get locally) and the painting supplies aren't going to go very far (maybe 10-20 rocks?). Still, this kit is enough to see if this is something your child enjoys. I painted the rock in the photo using the book instructions, but modifying the design to fit the rock.

text_fidelity_a: Power Wheels Kawasaki Lil' Quad The power wheels kawasaki lil' quad is a great toy for a toddler. You will want to make sure that your little one has enough flat space to drive around because the turning radius is extremely wide. You will need a very large space to make a complete circle. Also, there is no reverse button. You should not ride this near hills, slopes, pools, roads, cars, or anywhere else that could increase the chances of an accident. You should also note that even if the "go" button is not being pressed the quad can reach high speeds if on a steep incline.  It comes with a rechargeable 6v 4Ah battery and charging cord that is to be plugged into a wall outlet (not a ceiling outlet!). Before using for the first time the battery must be charged for 18 hours, and 14 hours after each use. You are warned not to leave the battery charging for longer than 30 hours or it may cause the battery to degrade. The biggest downside is that there is no light to denote the battery is charging or completely charged. You just have to assume it is charging and that the battery is completely charged after you unplug it. It requires about 10 minutes of assembly time (excluding the sticker time). The quad does not come with the stickers already placed, so you will need to place the stickers on yourself. You will need a philips head and a flat head screw driver, all other parts are included. The only problem that I noted was one of the connections would not completely engage. There is a wire that is used to connect the battery one end and then the electrical supply from the "go" but on the handlebar. For some reason I could not get the handlebar connection to completely snap into place. Even though it did not completely connect it was enough for everything to work, so I left it as is. I was afraid to force it to completely connect and potentially breaking the plastic connector. It is listed to be for 12-36 months, and up to 40 pounds. Personally, I think 12 months is a little young to be riding this, especially if your child is on the small side and not completely steady on their feet when walking. Made in China.
text_fidelity_b: Power Wheels Kawasaki Lil' Quad

I have only been using it for 4.8 volt and 7.2 volt packs so far but there has been no heat issues.  Directions are so-so.  If your new to this type of charger there are some videos that are much better than the written directions.  If you have used any type of programmable charge then this will be easy enough to figure out and use from just the written direction.  Love the auto battery test and the reverse polarity warning.  Makes this a much safer option.  The fireproof bag is large enough for most packs and Hopefully will never have to be tested.  I don't generally need to charge my batteries while away from an outlet but it is nice to know that this can handle that also.  Just very pleased with the entire package.

Hot Wheels 20-Pack of 1:64 Scale Toy Sports & Race Cars, Collectible Vehicles (Styles May Vary) It might seem as if 20 cars is too much at once. Nope! It is wonderful.

Days as a five year-old were best filled with playing in complete abandon. The freedom proffered by youth needed only a few toys to complete the ever-present joy. A few toys which mattered included several tattered but friendly books, a truck or two, an odd shovel and bucket, and, the coup de grace, a Hot Wheels car. Mattel makes a track as well, but a well-made car could take a boy places. This set of 20 is what kindergartners drool over.

A boy has everything in this set: vehicles of all colors, a few truck varieties, some funny looking cars. There are plenty, and frankly, since a few will invariably wind up lost under the couch, eaten by the dog, and buried with other treasures in the garden, having 20 quickly becomes justified.

Why a Hot Wheels car? Because they are made with hard steel. They are painted with a slick color. They hold up to frequent tastings, sand grindings, dirt smearings and other nonsense that comes with power racing in a sandbox. Sticky chocolate wipes off with warm water, and grime comes out with a good spray under the faucet.

The wheels themselves have a bounce peculiar to a genuine Hot Wheels vehicle. That's how my brother and I made sure it had adequate fuel. Ten bounces should be enough, we figured, and usually, we were right.

I fully recommend the "Hot Wheels 20-Car Gift Pack."

Anthony Trendl
AmericanSpeechwriter.com
text_fidelity_b: Hot Wheels 20-Pack of 1:64 Scale Toy Sports & Race Cars, Collectible Vehicles (Styles May Vary)

text_fidelity_a:
Ravensburger Zodiac 270 Piece Puzzle Ball I'm someone who will cheat at something if I can. Like when I was was a kid, and I played [[ASIN:B00000IWCT Monopoly]] with my little brothers, I would steal money from the bank, just because I could.

Each piece of this puzzle has a number on the back of it, and the numbers tell you which pieces fit together. So, it's much easier to flip over all of the pieces of the puzzle, and put it together upside down, that by putting the puzzle together by the picture. And it's much easier by a lot. I think that everyone who does this puzzle will eventually get frustrated, and resort to doing the puzzle upside down, which I consider 'cheating.'

It's very solid, and very strong, when you put it together. The pieces are made of sturdy plastic, not cardboard, like other puzzles. Also the pieces seem like they're cast, or molded, and not cut. That's why the globe surface ends up smooth. But, because all of the pieces were manufactured separately, instead as a whole puzzle, then the picture doesn't always match up from piece to piece.

It comes with a cheap stand, but it looks pretty nice when it's assembled and displayed. I hid a few coins in the middle of it, so it rattles when you move it. It's got lot of area in the middle for a small sphere, so it could double as a secret safe.

Pros:
+Very sturdy, especially when the sphere is completed
+Nice picture, with a bunch of cool zodiac symbols
+High quality

Cons:
-Has numbers on the back of each piece of the puzzle, so it's super simple to assemble
-Plastic, so it doesn't feel like a real puzzle
-The picture doesn't always line up from piece to piece
text_fidelity_b: Ravensburger Zodiac 270 Piece Puzzle Ball

text_fidelity_a:
Magic The Gathering: Arena of the Planeswalkers Game This is a great value for what you're paying. Essentially, this game is based on another very good game called Heroscape. You'll build an arena out of the little pieces in this box, create an army, and do battle with one of the prepainted Planeswalker minis.

I picked this game up as a former MtG player. I was hugely involved in the game from Ice Age through Darksteel. I invested thousands of dollars in the game until it finally became apparent that I couldn't afford to continue to be competitive in the game. What I love about this is that there is a little of what I like about MtG - the deckbuilding, the spellcasting and the strategy - but not so much of what I don't like - the cost.

The game itself is solid if not spectacular. It accomodates up to 5 relatively seamlessly, and it's easy to set up the game as a 2 vs. 2 if you like the team approach, or to just make it a free-for-all. The biggest problem to me with the game, enough to lower it two full stars, is that the game feels like it is missing some essential element that will be added through expansions. It's difficult to identify exactly what it is, but I can't shake the feeling that they took something essential out and going to release it as a big box expansion in the next few months.

As it is, it's a solid game that feels unfinished. I'll eagerly look forward to the (I"m assuming) forthcoming expansion.
text_fidelity_b: Magic The Gathering: Arena of the Planeswalkers Game

Journey Girls 18" Doll, Callie The Journey Girls dolls are 18" dolls. Clothing-wise, they appear to be compatible with other 18" dolls such as American Girl, Playtime by Eimmie, the Our Generation dolls, or even the 18" Adora dolls. At this price point, they are definitely an affordable play option for younger girls. Like the Adora dolls, they have plastic shoulder and upper torso area and the lower torso is cloth. (The AG, Playtime by Eimmie, and Our Generation dolls all have completely cloth torsos). The Journey Girls dolls do not turn their head well, but their face sculpts are all unique to each doll (again, similar to the Adora dolls, as the Playtime by Eimmie seem to all have the same face sculpt with different skin shades and paint jobs). I personally find the Adora dolls to be my favorite 18" alternative to the American Girl dolls, but they are still at a high enough price point that I would not want to hand one over to my 5 year old for unsupervised play. The Playtime by Eimmie dolls have a full cloth body, making them softer and more huggable than the Journey Girls dolls (and probably more appealing for younger girls), and they are about the same price point. The style of clothing the Journey Girls have, as well as their sculpted plastic upper torsos, they give the impression of teenagers rather than younger girls, which makes them very appealing to the 8-10 year old set.

The packaging indicated Callie is from Japan, and she definitely has more almond-shaped eyes than Meredith. Her light skin, brown hair (instead of black), and eye shape reminded my bi-racial girls of themselves. That is the true gift of doll lines that have unique face sculpts, to provide a mirror so all little girls can have a doll that resembles them, as well as a truly diverse line of dolls.
text_fidelity_b: Journey Girls 18" Doll, Callie

text_fidelity_a:
The Secret Life of Pets - Snowball Walking Talking Pets Figure This is a 'cute' little toy. I like the expression on his face. We've had fun playing with it for the past couple weeks.

Some things that you might want to know about it if you're considering buying one.

The instructions suggest replacing the two AAA batteries when you take the figure out of the package - the two that come in it are for 'in-store' demonstration purposes. Opening the battery compartment I found that the supplied batteries are pretty decent alkaline ones. Still, I replaced the ones in mine as I hate it when batteries go dead in a device and then leak. Something to maybe mention - the battery compartment is secured with a screw, so that small hands can't get into it.

The tail on the rabbit acts as the on/off switch. There are three setting - On, Off, and Demo. In the demonstration mode the figure talks and the wheels turn for a few seconds and then stops. When in the On position, the figure says a phrase - the wheels go for awhile and then it stops and repeats the cycle. The figure has three wheels - two fixed wheels seem to drive it's motion and a third rotates to make the figure go in different directions. Our rabbit seems to have a habit of finding the nearest corner and parking itself in it. The figure's eyes move a bit when it's in running around (although it's hard to see with the way it's eyes are set).

The figure comes with a separate carrot prop. Which the rabbit is suppose to hold in it's one hand - ours kept dropping his. So I took a piece of the white string that had secured the toy to the package and tied the carrot to his hand- you can't really even see it.

The rabbit talks, and I know it's suppose to be Kevin Hart doing a 'cartoon' voice - but it's really hard to understand what it's suppose to be saying. Hopefully when the movie comes out the phrases will be more recognizable.

All in all I like this figure and I'm looking forward to seeing the movie.
text_fidelity_b: The Secret Life of Pets - Snowball Walking Talking Pets Figure

Winning Moves Games Sorry Classic Edition Board Game, Multicolor [[VIDEOID:c9ed210fcea7bd15ff238268da66c6e5]] I really liked this classic game of Sorry. I hadn't played this game in over 25 years, so this is a fun blast from the past.

The game isn't as silly or as random as I remember it. For a random move your pawn game, there is actually a decent amount of strategy involved.

The rules were a bit confusing, since they used the old 1959 rules. Here's my summary of the rules: You can only move your pawns out of start if you pick a 1, 2, or sometimes a Sorry card. If you get a 1 or a 2, then you only move out to the first circle. You only slide when you get on the first part of the slide. If you can't move, you don't move, and you need an exact count to get into the Home square. Follow the rest of the instructions on the cards.

Pros:
+It's possible to win no matter how far behind a player is
+Great rendition of a classic game
+A lot of fun
+Great for any ages

Cons:
-The rules are a bit confusing. I had to clarify some of the rules on the internet.
-The game starts out very slowly
text_fidelity_b: Winning Moves Games Sorry Classic Edition Board Game, Multicolor

Fisher-Price Roar 'n Ride Lion [[VIDEOID:6d6cbfe820d25c4bf20272caa9cdc5e0]] My girlfriend said, "This is the kind of toy that you only get for your worst enemies." I, on the other hand love it! And, kids love it too. The problem with this is that it's a noise-making toy that is very fun and exciting if you're the one controlling it, but kind of annoying if you're not controlling it.

This is a play lion, that comes with suction cups to stick to the side of the car. When you press the lion's belly, then it makes some sounds. When you rattle something, like with the attached rattle, then it does extended music and sound. It's meant to teach kids that if they rattle something, then something else in the environment might react.

One big warning. This ships in Demo mode, where pressing the Lion's tummy works, but the rattle doesn't work. At first I thought it was broken. But, all you have to do is switch this off and then switch it back on, and then both the rattle and pressing the Lion's abdomen will work. And, speaking of switching this off, the switch is hidden on the lion's back, and is super hard to get to. And, it's impossible to change the batteries without ripping the lion's clothes.

Pros:
+Kids love it
+Great for teaching cause and effect
+Makes a lot of noise
+You can stick it on the window

Cons:
-Can be annoying for adults
-On/off switch and batteries are inconveniently located
-Isn't as fun if it's not stuck to a window
text_fidelity_b: Fisher-Price Roar 'n Ride Lion

Ben Franklin Toys Electronic Bill & Coin Counter Bank with LCD Screen, One Size This was a great idea, that totally failed.
The idea is good - you push coins through the slot, and it counts them. You want to add notes, fold them up, push them through the note slot, and press the button representing the value of the note. This is clever, as identifying notes is pretty expensive tech, and the buttons are easy enough to use.
If you push the coins through too quickly, they dont get counted - you have to push them as slowly as you can and even then it has a tenancy to thing quarters are pennys.
The reset button is unusually deep, it was easier to take the batteries out. Then, as you screw the lid back on, make sure you dont press one of the buttons, or you will be repeating the process.
Want to know how much money you have (assuming it counted it correctly?) to do this you have to add more money! There is no way to get it to tell you whats in it without adding to it.
It could be a lot of fun, and practical. Sadly its annoying and useless.
